newsitem.title: USA: Reynold's lawyer says late smoker made the choice.
newsitem.headline: Reynold's lawyer says late smoker made the choice.

text.p: The key issue in a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co was whether a woman who smoked cigarettes despite knowing about the possible health risks should be awarded damages because of her decision, a lawyer for the company said Wednesday.

In his opening statement, Paul Crist, representing Reynolds, outlined a five-point plan of attack against the lawsuit, filed by Dana Raulerson on behalf of the estate of her late sister, Jean Connor, who died of lung cancer.

Crist said the key issue was "whether someone who chose to smoke, despite more than 27 years of warnings on every pack of cigarettes she smoked ... and despite a barrage of media attention, should be awarded monetary damages because of that decision."

Conner filed a product liability suit against the tobacco company before her death from lung cancer in 1995 at age 49. The lawsuit became a wrongful death suit with Raulerson as the plaintiff after Connor died.

Crist said he would show there was a widespread awareness that smoking could be harmful to health, that warnings put on cigarette packages after 1969 were legally adequate, that cigarettes are legal, that smoking is a personal choice and that smokers are able to quit.

"Our society has already made the decision as to whether people are entitled to choose whether to smoke," Crist said, adding that there was plenty of information available to help them make intelligent decisions.

Crist's opening argument followed those of two lawyers for Raulerson, who said they would prove the tobacco company, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, knew it was selling a dangerous product but failed to properly warn customers and fix the product.
Testimony in the widely watched case was scheduled to begin Thursday with Dr. Allan Feingold, chief of pulmonary medicine at South Miami Hospital, on the witness stand.
In a final pretrial hearing last week, Reynolds lawyers successfully sought to curtail any extemporaneous commentary by Feingold, who has said publicly that he had no respect for cigarette companies.
Judge Bernard Nachman indicated he would make Feingold limit his answers to the questions he was asked.

Crist told jurors that he would provide evidence showing it was not clear whether Connor's cancer had started in her lungs, and that no autopsy was performed to prove where the cancer started, even though Connor had sued the tobacco company months before she died.
"They (plaintiffs) made a decision to deprive you of the most definitive evidence" about where the cancer started, he told the jury.

Crist said there was "astronomical" public awareness about the potential risks of cigarette smoking. He cited a 1954 Gallup poll in which 90 percent of respondents answered yes when asked whether they had heard or read anything that cigarette smoking may be a cause of lung cancer.
